title: Market Street Associates v. Frey
summary: Deliberately exploiting a contractual partner’s oversight could violate good faith, but the relevant state of mind could not be decided against the tenant on this summary-judgment record.
notes: The later finding reported at C&M p. 735 was that Orenstein initially expected the trust to review the lease, then realized it was not doing so and continued sending ambiguous requests until invoking the option. The editors report denial of specific performance on that later record. Keep that result separate from the appellate remand.

sections.Parties: Market Street Associates was a successor tenant under a sale-and-leaseback arrangement originally made by J.C. Penney with General Electric Pension Trust. It sought specific performance of an option to buy the leased property.
sections.Material Facts:
Paragraph 34 required the trust to give reasonable consideration to requests to finance improvements. If financing negotiations failed in the specified circumstances, the tenant could repurchase the property on a formula that could be favorable after substantial appreciation. About twenty years later, Market Street sought to buy the property so that it could obtain financing elsewhere.

After the trust’s representative was slow to respond, Market Street’s representative Orenstein sent two requests for $4 million in financing without mentioning paragraph 34. The trust replied that the request was below its $7 million minimum. More than a month later, Market Street invoked the purchase option. Orenstein testified that it had occurred to him that the trust’s representative might not know about paragraph 34, although he expected the trust to check its file. The parties disputed whether the financing requests were a deliberate attempt to trigger the option by exploiting that oversight.
sections.Procedural History: The district court entered summary judgment for the trust on the ground that Market Street had violated good faith. The Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded for trial on the relevant state of mind. The editors separately report that, after trial on remand, the district court found deliberate exploitation and denied specific performance.
sections.Issue: Did failing to call attention to paragraph 34 violate good faith, and could the court determine from this record that the omission was an opportunistic attempt to obtain the property?
sections.Holding: A deliberate attempt to take advantage of the trust’s oversight could violate good faith. The summary-judgment record did not establish that state of mind conclusively; a trial was required.
sections.Reasoning:
Good faith does not generally make contracting parties fiduciaries who must put the other side’s interests first. A party ordinarily may use superior market knowledge, protect its bargain, and decline to rescue a counterparty from financial difficulty. The court distinguished those forms of self-interest from deliberately using a partner’s ignorance of the existing contract to defeat the understanding on which their ongoing relationship rested.

If Orenstein believed the trust knew or would check the paragraph, he could request financing and later invoke the option without being required to provide unsolicited legal advice. If he intentionally induced a refusal by keeping the trust unaware of the paragraph, the same outward correspondence could amount to sharp dealing. Resolving that issue required an assessment of knowledge and purpose. The opinion therefore articulates a limit on performance behavior while preserving the procedural distinction between a plausible inference and a fact established after trial.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Market Street explains good faith through a particular misuse of an existing contractual mechanism. It also shows why a case’s procedural stage matters when its outcome depends on a person’s knowledge.

topics.good-faith: A party may protect its interests while remaining prohibited from deliberately exploiting a counterparty’s oversight of their existing agreement.
topics.discretion: The financing request and option mechanism had to be used consistently with the contractual relationship.
topics.disclosure: The case distinguishes general market-information advantages from exploiting ignorance of the existing contract.
topics.option-contracts: The tenant sought to trigger and exercise a contractual purchase option.
topics.specific-relief: Bad faith could defeat specific performance; the later trial found the relevant misconduct.

mnemonic.rationale: A lease clause the landlord forgot
